'''Brian McRae Barnes''' is a zoologist and an academic. His works have focused on [[hibernation]] science, [[biological rhythm]]s, [[Ecophysiology|physiological ecology]], [[comparative endocrinology]], and [[overwintering]] biology. He was appointed the inaugural Knut Schmidt-Nielsen Named Lecturer by the [[International Union of Physiological Sciences]] in 2009 and was elected a fellow by the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 2011.

==Education==
Barnes completed his [[Bachelor of Science|Bachelor's]] in Biology at the [[University of California, Riverside]] in 1977. He earned his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in [[Zoology]] from the [[University of Washington]] in 1983 in the lab of [[Jim Kenagy]].<ref name=gng>{{Cite web |url=https://people.iab.uaf.edu/brian_barnes/ |title=Brian Barnes |website=University of Alaska Fairbanks |access-date= September 11, 2025}}</ref>

==Career==
After training as a postdoc at the University of California, Berkeley under Irv Zucker and Paul Licht, Barnes began his career at the [[University of Alaska Fairbanks]] as an assistant professor of Zoophysiology in 1986. He was promoted to an associate professor in 1991 and a professor in 2000.<ref name = gng/> He was appointed as the Glaser Distinguished Professor at [[Florida International University]] in 2011.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://fiuglaser.fiu.edu/?cat=1 |title=FIU Glaser Professorships – Category 1 |website=Florida International University Glaser Professorship |date=2 October 2024 |access-date= September 11, 2025}}</ref>

From 2000 to 2020, Barnes was the director of the Institute of Arctic Biology. He was also the principal investigator for the Toolik Field Station's cooperative agreement with NSF<ref name=barn>{{Cite web|url=https://www.uaf.edu/aurora/archives/winter-2024/brian-barnes-burrows-into-retirement-after-nearly-40-years-at-uaf.php|title=Brian Barnes burrows into retirement after nearly 40 years at UAF|website=uaf.edu|access-date=November 10, 2025}}</ref> and was appointed as the director at the Alaska INBRE in 2014.<ref name = gng/> He has also served as both science director and co-science director of the Toolik Field Station in Arctic Alaska at the University of Alaska Fairbanks.<ref name = gng/><ref name=barn/>

==Research==
Barnes's work is mostly focused in the areas of hibernation science, biological rhythms, physiological ecology, comparative endocrinology, and overwintering biology.

===Hibernation science===
One of Barnes' earliest works involved the [[golden-mantled ground squirrel]]s and how their winter hibernation, particularly their torpor state, is related to their reproduction cycle.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Entwistle |first1=A. C. |last2=Racey |first2=P. A. |last3=Speakman |first3=J. R. |title=The reproductive cycle and determination of sexual maturity in male brown long-eared bats, Plecotus auritus (Chiroptera: Vespertilionidae) |journal=Journal of Zoology |date=January 1998 |volume=244 |issue=1 |pages=63–70|doi=10.1111/j.1469-7998.1998.tb00007.x |bibcode=1998JZoo..244...63E }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fietz |first1=Joanna |last2=Pflug |first2=M. |last3=Schlund |first3=W. |last4=Tataruch |first4=F. |title=Influences of the feeding ecology on body mass and possible implications for reproduction in the edible dormouse (Glis glis) |journal=Journal of Comparative Physiology B |date=January 2005 |volume=175 |issue=1 |pages=45–55 |doi=10.1007/s00360-004-0461-1 |pmid=15645237 |bibcode=2005JCmPB.175...45F }}</ref> He showed that seasonal reproductive maturation (puberty) in males requires that, while remaining in their [[Hibernaculum (zoology)|hibernacula]], males return to high body temperatures in spring one to three weeks before females emerge.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Thompson |first1=Megan J. |last2=Dobson |first2=F. Stephen |last3=Coltman |first3=David W. |last4=Murie |first4=Jan O. |last5=Raveh |first5=Shirley |last6=Lane |first6=Jeffrey E. |title=Sexes in sync: phenotypic plasticity, sexual selection and phenological synchrony between the sexes in a wild hibernator |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences |date=29 November 2023 |volume=290 |issue=2011 |article-number=20231113 |doi=10.1098/rspb.2023.1113 |pmid=37964523 |pmc=10646457 }}</ref> His early research on [[arctic ground squirrel]]s, published as the cover article in [[Science (journal)|Science Magazine]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Barnes |first1=Brian M. |title=Freeze Avoidance in a Mammal: Body Temperatures Below 0°C in an Arctic Hibernator |journal=Science |date=1989 |volume=244 |issue=4912 |pages=1593–1595 |doi=10.1126/science.2740905 |pmid=2740905 }}{{primary source inline|date=December 2025}}</ref> demonstrated that during hibernation, arctic ground squirrels<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Frank |first1=Craig L. |title=The Influence of Dietary Fatty Acids on Hibernation by Golden-Mantled Ground Squirrels (Spermophilus lateralis) |journal=Physiological Zoology |date=December 1992 |volume=65 |issue=5 |pages=906–920 |doi=10.1086/physzool.65.5.30158549 |jstor=30158549 |bibcode=1992PhysZ..65..906F }}</ref> regularly supercool their body to several degrees below the freezing point.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Arendt |first1=Thomas |last2=Stieler |first2=Jens T. |last3=Holzer |first3=Max |title=Tau and tauopathies |journal=Brain Research Bulletin |date=September 2016 |volume=126 |issue=Pt 3 |pages=238–292 |doi=10.1016/j.brainresbull.2016.08.018 |pmid=27615390 }}</ref> Along with his colleagues, he determined that during deep [[torpor]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Qiu |first1=M.-H. |last2=Chen |first2=M.C. |last3=Lu |first3=J. |title=Cortical neuronal activity does not regulate sleep homeostasis |journal=Neuroscience |date=June 2015 |volume=297 |pages=211–218 |doi=10.1016/j.neuroscience.2015.03.070 |pmid=25864961 |pmc=4428917 }}</ref> brain wave activity ceases,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kavanau |first1=J.Lee |title=Origin and Evolution of Sleep: Roles of Vision and Endothermy |journal=Brain Research Bulletin |date=1997 |volume=42 |issue=4 |pages=245–264 |doi=10.1016/s0361-9230(96)00331-0 |pmid=9043711 }}</ref> and that warming up from it<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Krystal |first1=Andrew D. |last2=Schopler |first2=Bobby |last3=Kobbe |first3=Susanne |last4=Williams |first4=Cathy |last5=Rakatondrainibe |first5=Hajanirina |last6=Yoder |first6=Anne D. |last7=Klopfer |first7=Peter |title=The Relationship of Sleep with Temperature and Metabolic Rate in a Hibernating Primate |journal=PLOS ONE |date=4 September 2013 |volume=8 |issue=9 |article-number=e69914 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0069914 |pmid=24023713 |pmc=3762832 |bibcode=2013PLoSO...869914K |doi-access=free }}</ref> causes squirrels to go from [[Non-rapid eye movement sleep|NREM]] to [[Rapid eye movement sleep|REM]] sleep before returning to the torpor state.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=The Temperature Dependence of Sleep |first1=David |last1=Harding |first2=Nicholas P. |last2=Franks |first3=William |last3=Wisden |journal=Frontiers in Neuroscience |volume=13 |article-number=336 |date= 2019 |doi=10.3389/fnins.2019.00336 |pmid=31105512 |pmc=6491889 |doi-access=free }}</ref> He has also conducted long-term studies of the daily and seasonal activity patterns in free-living arctic ground squirrels with the use of lightloggers.<ref>{{Cite ===Biological rhythms===
Barnes and his colleagues found in a study conducted on [[Winter white dwarf hamster|Siberian hamsters]] that the SCN-BAT connection is linked to torpor state, and that lesioning them results in the animal being unable to go back into it.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bamshad |first1=Maryam |last2=Song |first2=C. Kay |last3=Bartness |first3=Timothy J. |title=CNS origins of the sympathetic nervous system outflow to brown adipose tissue |journal=American Journal of Physiology. Regulatory, Integrative and Comparative Physiology |date=1999 |volume=276 |issue=6 |pages=R1569–R1578 |doi=10.1152/ajpregu.1999.276.6.R1569 |pmid=10362733 }}</ref> Along with Hut, he observed that periodically, the state of torpor is interrupted by short events of arousal where the core temperature of an animal is increased and most physiological functioning is restored.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fritze |first1=Marcus |last2=Costantini |first2=David |last3=Fickel |first3=Jörns |last4=Wehner |first4=Dana |last5=Czirják |first5=Gábor Á |last6=Voigt |first6=Christian C. |title=Immune response of hibernating European bats to a fungal challenge |journal=Biology Open |date=November 2019 |volume=8 |issue=10 |pages=bio046078 |doi=10.1242/bio.046078  |doi-access=free|doi-broken-date=19 December 2025 |pmid=31649120 |pmc=6826279 }}</ref> In another one of his studies, he and his colleagues implanted temperature data loggers to track the interbout arousals in Arctic ground squirrels.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Findlay-Robinson |first1=Rachel |last2=Deecke |first2=Volker B. |last3=Weatherall |first3=Andrew |last4=Hill |first4=Davina L. |title=Effects of climate change on life-history traits in hibernating mammals |journal=Mammal Review |date=2023 |volume=53 |issue=2 |pages=84–98 |doi=10.1111/mam.12308 |bibcode=2023MamRv..53...84F |doi-access=free }}</ref>

He also investigated how [[Abiotic component|abiotic conditions]] have an impact on the annual rhythms of a sample of various species, and how changes in said conditions can disturb them.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jones |first1=Matthew R. |last2=Mills |first2=L. Scott |last3=Alves |first3=Paulo Célio |last4=Callahan |first4=Colin M. |last5=Alves |first5=Joel M. |last6=Lafferty |first6=Diana J. R. |last7=Jiggins |first7=Francis M. |last8=Jensen |first8=Jeffrey D. |last9=Melo-Ferreira |first9=José |last10=Good |first10=Jeffrey M. |title=Adaptive introgression underlies polymorphic seasonal camouflage in snowshoe hares |journal=Science |date=2018 |volume=360 |issue=6395 |pages=1355–1358 |doi=10.1126/science.aar5273 |pmid=29930138 |bibcode=2018Sci...360.1355J |url=http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/258271 |hdl=10216/113397 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Moreover, he found that animal activity does not rely completely on [[circadian rhythm]]s and could happen around the clock in constant environments.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Animal clocks: when science meets nature|first1=Noga|last1=Kronfeld-Schor|first2=Guy|last2=Bloch|first3=William J.|last3=Schwartz|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences|volume=280|issue=1765|article-number=20131354|date=2013|doi=10.1098/rspb.2013.1354|pmid=23825215 |pmc=3712458 |bibcode=2013PBioS.28031354K }}</ref>

===Physiological ecology===
Focusing on physiological ecology, Barnes looked at how body mass loss remains the same in arctic ground squirrels, whether they are in colder or warmer burrows.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zervanos |first1=Stam M. |last2=Maher |first2=Christine R. |last3=Waldvogel |first3=Jerry A. |last4=Florant |first4=Gregory L. |title=Latitudinal Differences in the Hibernation Characteristics of Woodchucks ( ''Marmota monax'' ) |journal=Physiological and Biochemical Zoology |date=2010 |volume=83 |issue=1 |pages=135–141 |doi=10.1086/648736 |pmid=19958172 |bibcode=2010PhyBZ..83..135Z }}</ref> In related research on arctic ground squirrels, he also found that polysaccharated fatty acid levels in the diet have a small impact on their torpor patterns.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hulbert |first1=A. J. |last2=Abbott |first2=Sarah K. |title=Nutritional ecology of essential fatty acids: An evolutionary perspective |journal=Australian Journal of Zoology |date=2012 |volume=59 |issue=6 |pages=369–379 |doi=10.1071/ZO11064 }}</ref> His work on these squirrels also extends to the state of torpor as a response to the extreme Arctic cold and how it is briefly interrupted by interbout arousal or IBA every 3 weeks for rewarming.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Olsen |first1=Luke |last2=Thum |first2=Edward |last3=Rohner |first3=Nicolas |title=Lipid metabolism in adaptation to extreme nutritional challenges |journal=Developmental Cell |date=2021 |volume=56 |issue=10 |pages=1417–1429 |doi=10.1016/j.devcel.2021.02.024 |pmid=33730548 }}</ref>

===Comparative endocrinology===
Barnes has also conducted research on golden mantled squirrels, where he found that sperm maturation was temporarily linked to an increase in testosterone levels after hibernation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lilliendahl |first1=Kristjan |title=The effect of predator presence on body mass in captive greenfinches |journal=Animal Behaviour |date=1997 |volume=53 |issue=1 |pages=75–81 |doi=10.1006/anbe.1996.0279 |bibcode=1997AnBeh..53...75L }}</ref> Regarding hormones, he found that male arctic ground squirrels show an increased [[androgen]] level during peak breeding seasons and when encountering other males later in the spring.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Seasonal programming, not competition or testosterone, drives stress axis changes in male arctic ground squirrels|first1=Phoebe D.|last1=Edwards|first2=Rudolf Palme|last2=Palme|first3=Rudy|last3=Boonstra|journal=Hormones and Behavior|volume=85|pages=38–46|date=2016|doi=10.1016/j.yhbeh.2016.08.007 |pmid=27561227 }}</ref> His work has also pointed out how environmental cues like green-up and [[senescence]] are crucial for the [[Circannual cycle|circannual rhythm]] in small mammals.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Phenological synchronization of seasonal bird migration with vegetation greenness across dietary guilds|first1=Frank A.|last1=La Sorte|first2=Catherine H.|last2=Graham|journal=Journal of Animal Ecology|volume=90|issue=2|pages=343–355|date=2021|doi=10.1111/1365-2656.13345 |pmid=33107060 |bibcode=2021JAnEc..90..343L }}</ref>

===Overwintering biology===
Barnes' work also extends to insects, where in a study on insect blood or hemolymph, he and his colleagues found that at least 50 species of insects and spiders had [[Alpha-fetoprotein|Alpha-Fetoproteins]] in their blood.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Clark |first1=Melody S. |last2=Worland |first2=M. Roger |title=How insects survive the cold: Molecular mechanisms—a review |journal=Journal of Comparative Physiology B |date=2008 |volume=178 |issue=8 |pages=917–933 |doi=10.1007/s00360-008-0286-4 |pmid=18584182 |bibcode=2008JCmPB.178..917C }}</ref> He also investigated the physiology of the Alaska and Indiana variants of the [[Cucujus clavipes|Cucujus clavipes beetle]] where he found that the Alaskan variant had a lower [[Single-cell protein|SCP]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Duman |first1=John G. |title=Animal ice-binding (Antifreeze) proteins and glycolipids: An overview with emphasis on physiological function |journal=Journal of Experimental Biology |date=2015 |volume=218 |issue=12 |pages=1846–1855 |doi=10.1242/jeb.116905 |pmid=26085662 |bibcode=2015JExpB.218.1846D }}</ref> He also contributed to the discovery of a [[Xylomannan|xylomannan-based]] antifreeze [[glycolipid]] in the darkling beetle [[Upis ceramboides]].<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Icephobic/anti-icing properties of micro/nanostructured surfaces|first1=Ilja K.|last1=Voets|journal=Soft Matter|volume=13|issue=17|pages=3089–3103|date=2017|doi=10.1039/C6SM02867E|pmid=28657626 |pmc=5708349 }}</ref> He also highlighted that wood frogs overwintering in Alaska experience the coldest temperatures experienced by frog species,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Duman |first1=John G. |title=Animal ice-binding (antifreeze) proteins and glycolipids: an overview with emphasis on physiological function |journal=Journal of Experimental Biology |date=1 June 2015 |volume=218 |issue=12 |pages=1846–1855 |doi=10.1242/jeb.116905 |pmid=26085662 |bibcode=2015JExpB.218.1846D }}</ref> and noted the importance of cryprotectants in surviving freeze-thaw cycles.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bodu |first1=Mustafa |last2=Hitit |first2=Mustafa |last3=Greenwood |first3=Olivia Chika |last4=Murray |first4=Raheem Davian |last5=Memili |first5=Erdogan |title=Extender development for optimal cryopreservation of buck sperm to increase reproductive efficiency of goats |journal=Frontiers in Veterinary Science |date=2 April 2025 |volume=12 |article-number=1554771 |doi=10.3389/fvets.2025.1554771 |pmid=40241808 |pmc=12001040 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Moreover, he found that therapeutic interventions increased the creature's cryotolerance, staying frozen for as long as 218 days.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lewis |first1=Jedediah K. |last2=Bischof |first2=John C. |last3=Braslavsky |first3=Ido |last4=Brockbank |first4=Kelvin G.M. |last5=Fahy |first5=Gregory M. |last6=Fuller |first6=Barry J. |last7=Rabin |first7=Yoed |last8=Tocchio |first8=Alessandro |last9=Woods |first9=Erik J. |last10=Wowk |first10=Brian G. |last11=Acker |first11=Jason P. |last12=Giwa |first12=Sebastian |title=The Grand Challenges of Organ Banking: Proceedings from the first global summit on complex tissue cryopreservation |journal=Cryobiology |date=2016 |volume=72 |issue=2 |pages=169–182 |doi=10.1016/j.cryobiol.2015.12.001 |pmid=26687388 }}</ref>
